items.prompt: What is the main visible difference between a broadleaf tree and a conifer?

options.label: Broadleaf trees have wide, flat leaves, while conifers have needles or scales.
options.feedback: That's right—the leaf shape is the clearest way to tell them apart; broad leaves are flat and wide, conifer needles are thin or scale-like.

options.label: Broadleaf trees are always taller than conifers.
options.feedback: Not necessarily—height varies within each group; some conifers like redwoods are the tallest trees of all.

options.label: Broadleaf trees lose all their leaves every winter, while conifers never shed any needles.
options.feedback: That's not exact—many broadleaf trees are evergreen too, and conifers do shed old needles gradually; the real distinction is leaf shape.

options.label: Broadleaf trees have cones, while conifers have flowers.
options.feedback: It's the opposite—conifers bear cones, while broadleaf trees typically produce flowers and often fruits.

items.ok_line: Broad leaves are flat; conifer needles are thin or scale-like.
items.ko_line: Height varies within both groups, so it can't separate them.
items.exp_text: The most straightforward way to tell a broadleaf tree from a conifer is by its leaves: broadleaf trees carry wide, flat blades, while conifers carry needles or small scales. This difference in leaf shape drives many other contrasts in how the trees live.

items.prompt: What do conifers use to reproduce instead of flowers?

options.label: Seeds inside fleshy fruits
options.feedback: Fleshy fruits come from flowering plants, which is the broadleaf side, not from conifers—though some conifers have berry-like cones, those are still cones.

options.label: Cones
options.feedback: Yes—conifers reproduce by forming cones that hold their seeds, which is why they are often called cone-bearing trees.

options.label: Spores like ferns
options.feedback: Spores are used by ferns and mosses, not by conifers; conifers produce seeds in cones.

options.label: Tiny flowers hidden under the bark
options.feedback: Hide-and-seek isn't how it works—conifers don't have flowers at all; they rely on cones for reproduction.

items.ko_line: No conifer produces flowers; cones are the reproductive structure.
items.exp_text: Conifers are named for their cones—woody or berry-like structures that hold the seeds. Unlike broadleaf trees, which often flower and fruit, conifers depend on cones for reproduction.

items.prompt: Which of these is a typical broadleaf tree?

options.label: Spruce
options.feedback: Spruce is a conifer, with needles and cones, not a broadleaf tree.

options.label: Pine
options.feedback: Pine is a classic conifer, bearing needles in bundles and cones.

options.label: Oak
options.feedback: Oak is a broadleaf tree—it has wide, lobed leaves and produces acorns, which are its fruits.

options.label: Fir
options.feedback: Fir is another conifer, with flat needles attached individually, but it still belongs to the cone-bearing group.

items.ok_line: Oak has wide leaves and acorns.
items.ko_line: Those three all carry needles and cones.
items.exp_text: An oak is a broadleaf tree, recognised by its broad, flat leaves and its acorn fruits. Spruce, pine and fir are all conifers, with needle-like leaves and cones.

items.prompt: What shape is the leaf of most conifers?

options.label: Needle-like or scale-like
options.feedback: Exactly—conifer leaves are thin needles or small overlapping scales, which help reduce water loss.

options.label: Broad and flat
options.feedback: That's the broadleaf pattern, not the conifer one—broad leaves lose more water.

options.label: Round and fleshy
options.feedback: Round, fleshy leaves belong to some desert plants, not to typical conifers.

options.label: Heart-shaped
options.feedback: Heart-shaped leaves are found on some broadleaf species, like linden, not on conifers.

items.ok_line: Conifer leaves are long and thin or small and flat.
items.ko_line: Broad, flat leaves are the opposite of what conifers have.
items.exp_text: Conifer leaves are usually needle-shaped—long and narrow—or scale-like, tiny and overlapping. This shape limits water loss and helps the tree survive in dry or cold conditions.

items.prompt: What is the typical crown shape of a conifer like a spruce or fir?

options.label: Wide and rounded
options.feedback: A wide rounded crown is more typical of broadleaf trees, which branch out broadly—conifers tend to be narrower.

options.label: Cone-shaped with a pointed top
options.feedback: Yes—spruces and firs form a cone or Christmas-tree shape, with a single straight trunk and a pointed peak.

options.label: Flat-topped and spreading
options.feedback: A flat top sometimes appears in old broadleaf trees or in some palms, not in typical spruces or firs.

options.label: Umbrella-shaped
options.feedback: An umbrella shape is found in some tropical trees, not in most conifers.

items.ok_line: Spruces and firs taper to a point at the top.
items.ko_line: Their crowns are narrow and pointed, not broad or flat.
items.exp_text: Most conifers, especially spruces and firs, grow a cone-shaped crown with a single straight trunk and a pointed tip. This shape sheds snow easily and lets the tree stand upright in harsh winters.

items.prompt: What substance do conifers produce that helps seal wounds and repel insects?

options.label: Nectar
options.feedback: Nectar is a sweet liquid made by flowers to attract pollinators, not a wound-sealing resin.

options.label: Sap that is always watery
options.feedback: Sap is the plant's transport fluid, but conifers also make a thick, sticky resin—it's the resin that seals and repels.

options.label: Wax
options.feedback: Wax coats the needles to reduce water loss, but it's resin inside the trunk that plugs cuts and deters insects.

options.label: Resin
options.feedback: That's correct—conifers produce sticky resin that flows out of any wound, hardens to seal it, and smells strong enough to discourage many insects.

items.ok_line: Conifers ooze resin to patch damage and fend off pests.
items.ko_line: Nectar attracts pollinators, and wax only coats the needles—resin does the sealing.
items.exp_text: Resin is the thick, aromatic substance that fills wounds in a conifer's trunk or branches. It hardens on contact with air, closing the cut and acting as a barrier against insects and fungi.

items.prompt: Which tree type typically has wood that is softer and easier to saw?

options.label: Conifer
options.feedback: Right—conifer wood is generally softer and lighter, which is why it's called softwood, even though some broadleaf woods are actually softer.

options.label: Broadleaf
options.feedback: Broadleaf wood is usually harder and denser, earning it the name hardwood, though exceptions exist.

options.label: Both equally
options.feedback: They differ—conifer wood is typically softer, broadleaf wood typically harder, on average.

options.label: Depends only on the age of the tree
options.feedback: Age doesn't decide the soft- or hardwood label; the tree type does, even if individual species vary.

items.ok_line: Typical conifer wood is softer to cut.
items.ko_line: Broadleaf wood tends to be denser, hence hardwood.
items.exp_text: Conifer wood is commonly called softwood because it's generally softer, lighter and easier to saw than broadleaf wood, which earns the name hardwood. The names come from the tree group, not from measuring every piece.

items.prompt: When do most broadleaf trees in temperate regions drop their leaves?

options.label: In spring
options.feedback: Spring is when new leaves appear, not when they fall—leaf drop happens in autumn for these trees.

options.label: In summer
options.feedback: Summer is the growing season; leaves stay on throughout, unless drought causes early drop.

options.label: In autumn
options.feedback: Yes—most temperate broadleaf trees shed their leaves in autumn, preparing for winter's cold and dryness.

options.label: They never drop them
options.feedback: Many temperate broadleaf trees are deciduous and do drop leaves each autumn; only evergreens hold theirs year-round.

items.ok_line: Temperate broadleaf trees lose leaves in autumn.
items.ko_line: Spring and summer are for new leaves and growth, not shedding.
items.exp_text: Most broadleaf trees in temperate regions are deciduous, meaning they drop all their leaves in autumn. This reduces water loss and damage when winter brings cold, dry air.

items.prompt: Which leaf type typically lasts for several years on the tree before being shed?

options.label: Broad leaves of an oak
options.feedback: Oak leaves usually last one season and fall each autumn—they are not multi-year leaves.

options.label: Needles of a pine
options.feedback: Yes—many pine needles stay attached for two to five years, slowly being replaced, so the tree stays green throughout the year.

options.label: Leaves of a maple
options.feedback: Maple leaves are annual, dropping every autumn, not lasting several years.

options.label: Leaves of a beech in winter
options.feedback: Beech often keeps dry leaves through winter, but they are dead and fall in spring—they don't live several years.

items.ok_line: Conifer needles live for years, not one season.
items.ko_line: Oak and maple leaves drop yearly, unlike pine needles.
items.exp_text: Conifer needles are built to last, often staying green for several years before they brown and drop. This is why conifers look green all winter, while broadleaf trees stand bare.

items.prompt: What does a conifer's narrow, needle-shaped leaf help it do?

options.label: Capture more sunlight than any broad leaf
options.feedback: Narrow needles don't capture more light per leaf—their advantage is water conservation, not extra light capture.

options.label: Grow faster in the shade
options.feedback: Needles don't help shade growth; broad leaves are better at gathering low light, but that's not the needle's job.

options.label: Store large amounts of water inside
options.feedback: Needles are thin, so they hold little water—they reduce water loss, they don't store much.

options.label: Reduce water loss
options.feedback: Yes—the small, waxy surface of a needle limits the amount of water that evaporates, helping the tree survive dry or freezing periods when roots can't draw water.

items.ok_line: Needles limit evaporation so the tree stays hydrated.
items.ko_line: Light capture comes from many needles working together, not from each needle alone.
items.exp_text: A narrow needle has far less surface area than a broad leaf, so far less water escapes through it. That's a key advantage for conifers in dry, windy or frozen conditions where water is hard to get.
